newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu blames Arafat for failing to stop violence.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu blames Arafat for failing to stop violence.

text.p: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Yasser Arafat Thursday of having done "damn all" to stamp out Palestinian violence and said the world had been soft on him on peace deal violations.
"I think the Palestinian Authority has had a very free ride. Basically the line was what they do is okay and the obstacle to peace is on this side," Netanyahu said.

Speaking in a Reuters interview a day after two Arab suicide bombers killed 13 people in Jerusalem's main Jewish market, he said the international community had an obligation to demand action from Palestinian President Arafat againist "terrorism."

"I insist on a real peace and it begins with Arafat's battle against terrorism. That is what the international community, that is what the European Community...has now the obligation to demand. It hasn't done so far, up to now," he said.
Asked whether he was proposing a block on foreign aid to Palestinian self-rule areas to press Arafat into action, Netanyahu said:
"Peace doesn't mean anything if boys and girls are being blown to smithereens by people who come from the area of your peace partner who does damn all about it.

"That's got to change and I think the international community can tell Arafat we want to help, it's important to help but we insist that you help yourself first and help the peace process by fighting terrorism."
Netanyahu has faced foreign criticism for pushing ahead in March with a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in a decision that brought deadlock to Israeli-PLO peacemaking.

He responded to Wednesday's killings by declaring a halt to peace talks until Arafat acted to end violence by Moslem militants. He said in Thursday's interview that the peace process could continue "and I believe it will continue if the Palestinian Authority does what it promised to do."
"A real contract is one that's kept by both sides. So far we've been doing the keeping, they've been doing the violating. That is not a prescription to go forward," Netanyahu said.
"I expect Mr Arafat to do what he promised to do and has failed to do so far and that is to fight these terrorists."

He rejected as "nonsense" Palestinian charges that an Israeli security clampdown barring Palestinians from entering Israel was a form of collective punishment and could lead to Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdaineh said separately that Israel's decisions following the suicide bombings were "a declaration of war" against Palestinians and that Israel had brought Wednesday's killings on itself through hardline policies that were frustrating peace efforts.
Netanyahu confirmed he had blocked the transfer of funds owed to the Palestinian Authority following the attack.
He also said Israel would arrest Arafat's police chief Ghazi Jabali, accused by the Israelis of organising attacks on Jewish settlers on the West Bank, if he left Palestinian territory.

He declined to elaborate on comments earlier by aides that Israel would re-enter areas it handed over to Palestinian self-rule under interim peace accords since 1993 to capture militants unless Arafat clamped down himself.
"We have every right to take the actions necessary to defend our citizens and we will do so," Netanyahu said.

Netanyahu has made clear his dislike of interim peace deals with the Palestinians signed by previous Labour governments but the leader of the right-wing Likud bloc said he had agreed to honour them since his election in May last year.
He rejected what he said was the argument that "progress for peace" would end violence.
"When did we have the greatest bursts of terrorism here in the Middle East? It was under the first three years of the Oslo accords under the Labour government," Netanyahu said.
"It gave and gave and gave, tried to placate the terrorists with everything they could think of. It didn't help...The first bulwark of peace is fighting terrorism."
Wednesday's bombings were the worst attack in Israel since Netanyahu's election and the deadliest since a series of suicide bombings in February and March 1996.

In an interview later on Thursday on CNN television's "Larry King Live," the Israeli prime minister said he had told Arafat when he called to express his condolences after the bombing that he appreciated his words but "we must have a 180 degree change in policy."

He said he urged Arafat to create "a climate of peace" so that negotiations could proceed. "We expect a change of rhetoric, a change of action, a change of words and a change of deeds," Netanyahu said.
Asked if the bombing was a major setback to peace talks, Netanyahu said, "Thirteen people blown to smithereens is a major setback to peace."
